messages.subject: Modifying themes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

Some updates on the theme system

I've implemented the + operator for themes:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/573/files#diff-9

Now you can do things like:
  theme_bw() + opts(axis.title.x = element_text(colour='red'))

I've also updated theme_bw() to use it:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/573/files#diff-12

The next steps are to deal with theme_update and update_element. I've always found it kind of confusing to work with them. Here are some changes that I think would be beneficial:

* Get rid of theme_update and update_element.
* Add an operator like %|%, which can be used to update individual properties of elements. For example:
  mytheme <- theme_bw()
  mytheme <- mytheme | opts(text = element_text(colour="red"))

One consequence of removing update_theme and update_element is that the current theme can't be modified in place. You'd have to do something like the above, and then:
  theme_set(mytheme)

Thoughts? I'm not sure if these changes should go in 0.9.2 because they'll break some functionality. But I suspect that people don't use theme_update and update_element very often anyway.

-Winston

On 6/5/2012 11:33 AM, joran wrote:
> On Tuesday, June 5, 2012 11:22:09 AM UTC-7, Winston Chang wrote:
>>
>> This is probably related to https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/550.
>>
>> I'm not sure of a good general solution, though. The question is, how do
>> distinguish between cases where the data really does have a small range,
>> and cases where the data all (ideally) has the same value, but with some
>> rounding error?
>>
>
> As a way out of that dilemma, would it make sense to simply switch when
> ggplot will behave "unexpectedly"? i.e. have ggplot assume by default that
> the data really do have a very small range, so that the bug is shifted to
> the case when the values really are all the same, but appear different due
> to rounding error? Isn't that what R's base graphics does?
>
> That seems like a more sensible default behavior to me, I suppose.

A previous fix (issue #6 in the scales package, commit e130daa), changed
the algorithm from:

if (length(x) == 1) return(TRUE)
x <- x / mean(x)
isTRUE(all.equal(x[1], x[2]))

to:

length(x) == 1 || isTRUE(all.equal(x[1] - x[2], 0))

Presumably to deal with "large numbers with small differences" (based on
the added tests).

The use of all.equal is to say "equal to within what is probably just
differences due to floating point representation" (my paraphrase).  From
the actual documentation of all.equal:

Numerical comparisons for scale = NULL (the default) are done by first
computing the mean absolute difference of the two numerical vectors. If
this is smaller than tolerance or not finite, absolute differences are
used, otherwise relative differences scaled by the mean absolute
difference.

By default, tolerance is .Machine$double.eps ^ 0.5 (which is
1.490116e-08 on my machine).

The old way only looked a relative difference, the new way looks at
absolute or relative difference (though reading the documentation of
all.equal, I'm still not sure I understand when it does which).

Ultimately, we need more tests cases. Pulling from the existing tests,
the two StackOverflow questions, and some others, I think these are right:

expect_false(zero_range(c(5.63e-147, 5.93e-123)))
expect_false(zero_range(c(-7.254574e-11, 6.035387e-11)))
expect_false(zero_range(c(1330020857.8787, 1330020866.8787)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(1330020857.8787, 1330020857.8787)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(1330020857.8787, 1330020857.8787*(1+1e-20))))
expect_false(zero_range(c(0,10)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(0,0)))
expect_false(zero_range(c(-1,1)))
expect_false(zero_range(c(-1,1*(1+1e-20))))
expect_false(zero_range(c(-1,1)*1e-100))
expect_false(zero_range(c(0,1)*1e-100))
expect_true(zero_range(c(1)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(0)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(1e100)))
expect_true(zero_range(c(1e-100)))

If so, here is a function which meets that criteria:

zero_range <- function(x) {
     m <- mean(x)
     if(m == 0L) {
         if (x[[1]] == 0L) {
             m <- 1
         } else {
             m <- x[[1]]
         }
     }
     length(x) == 1 || isTRUE(all.equal(diff(x/m), 0,
tolerance=.Machine$double.eps))
}

First, I change the tolerance to .Machine$double.eps, not the square
root of it.  Second, I rescale the vector based on the mean value, after
checking that it is not exactly 0L to take care of absolute size
differences. If the mean is exactly 0L, then rescale by the first value
(if it is not 0L); if both the mean and first value are exactly 0L,
don't rescale (since all are zero).

Any other tests to throw at this? Can anyone break it? (Other than with
length(x) > 2, but that is part of the documentation).

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

I went ahead and implemented a | operator for modifying element properties. Now you can do this to modify specified properties of theme elements:
  mytheme <- theme_bw() | opts(text=element_text(colour='red'))
  qplot(1:3, 1:3) + mytheme

Notice that this is different from using +, which replaces the whole element. For example, this won't work because text properties like size, family, etc, are NULL:
  mytheme <- theme_bw() + opts(text=element_text(colour='red'))
  qplot(1:3, 1:3) + mytheme

So far, so good. But the syntax for adding to a ggplot object (not yet implemented) would look a little weird. For example:
  qplot(1:3, 1:3) | opts(text=element_text(colour='red'))

One possible solution is, instead of using things like this:
  mytheme | opts(...)
  qplot(...) | opts(...)
it could be implemented by adding a new function, modopts():
  mytheme + modopts(...)
  qplot(...) + modopts(...)

Thoughts?

-Winston

The + operator is great. It's very natural in ggplot's syntax, congrats.

But, like Brian, I'm not sure I understand the point of the %|% operator and even if it is what I think it is (replace just one element of a base property), I don't think it should exist as such, I think it should just work with + (easy to say, probably less to implement but well, you asked for feedback ;) )

The key is probably to be able to use element_*** on a base property of the theme (e.g. element_text on text) *without specifying everything*. Maybe all the base properties should exist outside of any theme or in the theme function arguments, so that it is always possible to fall back on them?

Also, in Brian's example:

opts(text = element_text(... something appropriate ...),
    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), angle=45),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour="green"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour="red", angle=90))

+ opts(axis.text.y = element_text(colour="purple"))

I think the y axis text should be 0.8 times the base size, at 90º and purple, i.e. each modification should be incremental.

In your implementation of + for themes you write:
	# Can't use modifyList here since it works recursively and drops NULLs
I think this is exactly what + should do though: modify the appropriate list element, dropping NULLs (alternatively the element_*** functions could only return non NULL items but that would probably be more cumbersome to implement). The sequence of modifications in the example above should be equivalent to doing:

mytheme$axis.text$size = rel(0.8)
mytheme$axis.text$angle = 45
mytheme$axis.text.x$colour = "green"
mytheme$axis.text.y$colour = "red"
mytheme$axis.text.y$angle = 90
mytheme$axis.text.y$colour = "purple"

and only this.

Ideally, I would advocate for this:
- the theme is a list of lists, with either
	. only the defined properties at each level (that would be cleaner to display)
	. or NULL for undefined properties at each level (this is probably easier to implement and work with)
- each element of the list can be modified independently, including the base elements, using the usual $ syntax
- the element_*** functions just allow to make those same modifications through functions, which help checking that the arguments are correct (it's not done at the moment though, but I guess this was the appeal of using functions, otherwise $ really seems more practical)
- the + operator works with lists of objects of class "element" (opts() calls basically) and can be used with ggplots
	ggplot(...) + geom_***(...) + opts(axis.text=element_text(...))
or themes
	theme_grey(...) + opts(axis.text=element_text(...))

What do you guys think?

PS: additional questions : besides theme elements, what can opts be used for? I see title but that's about it. If that's the case maybe another name would be more appropriate.

You need to distinguish between

element_text(colour = NULL)

and

element_text()

which both produce the same output - i.e. you need to distinguish
between saying that the element should inherit from its parent, vs
stay unchanged.  I think the clearest behaviour (in line with how
scales work) is for:

+ element_text(colour = NULL)

to leave the colour unchanged and

+ element_text(colour = inherit())

to force colour to be inherited from the parent.

One other thing we'd need to make clear is that

+ element_text(size = rel(0.8)) + element_text(size = rel(0.5))

gives a text size of 0.5 relative to it's parent, not 0.8 * 0.5 = 0.4.

On Wed, Jun 6, 2012 at 12:58 AM, Jean-Olivier Irisson <iri...@normalesup.org> wrote:
> On 2012-Jun-05, at 23:36 , Winston Chang wrote:
> >
> >> I've implemented the + operator for themes:
> >> https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/573/files#diff-9
> >> [...]
> >> Thoughts? I'm not sure if these changes should go in 0.9.2 because they'll break some functionality. But I suspect that people don't use theme_update and update_element very often anyway.
> >
> > I went ahead and implemented a | operator for modifying element properties. Now you can do this to modify specified properties of theme elements:
> >   mytheme <- theme_bw() | opts(text=element_text(colour='red'))
> >   qplot(1:3, 1:3) + mytheme
> >
> > Notice that this is different from using +, which replaces the whole element. For example, this won't work because text properties like size, family, etc, are NULL:
> >   mytheme <- theme_bw() + opts(text=element_text(colour='red'))
> >   qplot(1:3, 1:3) + mytheme
>
> The + operator is great. It's very natural in ggplot's syntax, congrats.
>
> But, like Brian, I'm not sure I understand the point of the %|% operator and even if it is what I think it is (replace just one element of a base property), I don't think it should exist as such, I think it should just work with + (easy to say, probably less to implement but well, you asked for feedback ;) )
>
> The key is probably to be able to use element_*** on a base property of the theme (e.g. element_text on text) *without specifying everything*. Maybe all the base properties should exist outside of any theme or in the theme function arguments, so that it is always possible to fall back on them?
>
>
> Also, in Brian's example:
>
> opts(text = element_text(... something appropriate ...),
>    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), angle=45),
>    axis.text.x = element_text(colour="green"),
>    axis.text.y = element_text(colour="red", angle=90))
> + opts(axis.text.y = element_text(colour="purple"))
>
> I think the y axis text should be 0.8 times the base size, at 90º and purple, i.e. each modification should be incremental.
>
> In your implementation of + for themes you write:
>        # Can't use modifyList here since it works recursively and drops NULLs
> I think this is exactly what + should do though: modify the appropriate list element, dropping NULLs (alternatively the element_*** functions could only return non NULL items but that would probably be more cumbersome to implement). The sequence of modifications in the example above should be equivalent to doing:
>
> mytheme$axis.text$size = rel(0.8)
> mytheme$axis.text$angle = 45
> mytheme$axis.text.x$colour = "green"
> mytheme$axis.text.y$colour = "red"
> mytheme$axis.text.y$angle = 90
> mytheme$axis.text.y$colour = "purple"
>
> and only this.
>
>
> Ideally, I would advocate for this:
> - the theme is a list of lists, with either
>        . only the defined properties at each level (that would be cleaner to display)
>        . or NULL for undefined properties at each level (this is probably easier to implement and work with)
> - each element of the list can be modified independently, including the base elements, using the usual $ syntax
> - the element_*** functions just allow to make those same modifications through functions, which help checking that the arguments are correct (it's not done at the moment though, but I guess this was the appeal of using functions, otherwise $ really seems more practical)
> - the + operator works with lists of objects of class "element" (opts() calls basically) and can be used with ggplots
>        ggplot(...) + geom_***(...) + opts(axis.text=element_text(...))
> or themes
>        theme_grey(...) + opts(axis.text=element_text(...))
>
> What do you guys think?
>
> PS: additional questions : besides theme elements, what can opts be used for? I see title but that's about it. If that's the case maybe another name would be more appropriate.
>

Here are some examples to illustrate how it all works. First, note that there's the elements in the theme object may have NULL properties -- if you access them directly, you'll see that the (non-root) elements are like this. The calc_element function figures out the properties with inheritance.

mytheme <-theme_grey() +
  opts(

    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), angle=45),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour="green"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour="red", angle=90))

mytheme$text
# List of 8
#  $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
#  $ face      : chr "plain"
#  $ colour    : chr "black"
#  $ size      : num 12
#  $ hjust     : num 0.5
#  $ vjust     : num 0.5
#  $ angle     : num 0
#  $ lineheight: num 0.9
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

mytheme$axis.text
# List of 8
#  $ family    : NULL
#  $ face      : NULL
#  $ colour    : NULL
#  $ size      :Class 'rel'  num 0.8
#  $ hjust     : NULL
#  $ vjust     : NULL
#  $ angle     : num 45
#  $ lineheight: NULL
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

mytheme$axis.text.y
# List of 8
#  $ family    : NULL
#  $ face      : NULL
#  $ colour    : chr "red"
#  $ size      : NULL
#  $ hjust     : NULL
#  $ vjust     : NULL
#  $ angle     : num 90
#  $ lineheight: NULL
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

Here's what the calc_element function does:

# 'text' is unchanged
calc_element("text", mytheme)
# List of 8
#  $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
#  $ face      : chr "plain"
#  $ colour    : chr "black"
#  $ size      : num 12
#  $ hjust     : num 0.5
#  $ vjust     : num 0.5
#  $ angle     : num 0
#  $ lineheight: num 0.9
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

calc_element("axis.text", mytheme)
# List of 8
#  $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
#  $ face      : chr "plain"
#  $ colour    : chr "black"
#  $ size      : num 9.6
#  $ hjust     : num 0.5
#  $ vjust     : num 0.5
#  $ angle     : num 45
#  $ lineheight: num 0.9
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

calc_element("axis.text.y", mytheme)
# List of 8
#  $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
#  $ face      : chr "plain"
#  $ colour    : chr "red"
#  $ size      : num 9.6
#  $ hjust     : num 0.5
#  $ vjust     : num 0.5
#  $ angle     : num 90
#  $ lineheight: num 0.9
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

The issue with the + operator is that it replaces the element entirely. Suppose I want to change my base 'text' element so that it is red. If I don't define all the element properties, I get a bunch of NULLs, which is a problem for a root node:

mytheme <- theme_grey() + opts(text = element_text(colour='red'))
mytheme$text
# List of 8
#  $ family    : NULL
#  $ face      : NULL
#  $ colour    : chr "red"
#  $ size      : NULL
#  $ hjust     : NULL
#  $ vjust     : NULL
#  $ angle     : NULL
#  $ lineheight: NULL
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

# calc_element throws an error in this case
calc_element("text", mytheme)
# Error in calc_element("text", mytheme) :
#   Theme element text has NULL property: family, face, size, hjust, vjust, angle, lineheight

The purpose of the | operator is to change just a single property, without throwing out all the others. For example:

mytheme <- theme_grey() | opts(text = element_text(colour='red'))
mytheme$text
# List of 8
#  $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
#  $ face      : chr "plain"
#  $ colour    : chr "red"
#  $ size      : num 12
#  $ hjust     : num 0.5
#  $ vjust     : num 0.5
#  $ angle     : num 0
#  $ lineheight: num 0.9
#  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

It can also be used on non-root elements to change a single property. For example, in theme_grey, 'axis.text' is defined as:
    axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), colour = "grey50")

To change just the color (and not the size), you could do:
   mytheme <- theme_grey() | opts(axis.text = element_text(colour="red"))

I can see how this syntax could be confusing, though.

Using J-O and Hadley's suggestions, the + operator would behave like the | operator presently does, except that there would be an inherit() value that specifically means to inherit this from the parent.

In general I think this makes sense, but it could potentially break exisiting code since it changes the behavior of the + operator.

-Winston

After some discussion with Hadley, here's what I ended up doing. The + operator replaces a specific properties of elements. There's also a %+replace% operator, which replaces the entire element. This operator probably will not see much use, except by someone who is creating a theme. See the definition of theme_bw() for an example: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/573/files#L22R67

> mytheme <- theme_grey() + theme(text = element_text(colour='red'))
> mytheme$text
List of 8
 $ family    : chr "Helvetica"
 $ face      : chr "plain"
 $ colour    : chr "red"
 $ size      : num 12
 $ hjust     : num 0.5
 $ vjust     : num 0.5
 $ angle     : num 0
 $ lineheight: num 0.9

 - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

> mytheme <- theme_grey() %+replace% theme(text = element_text(colour='red'))
> mytheme$text
List of 8
 $ family    : NULL
 $ face      : NULL
 $ colour    : chr "red"
 $ size      : NULL
 $ hjust     : NULL
 $ vjust     : NULL
 $ angle     : NULL
 $ lineheight: NULL

 - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

There are a lot of changes under the hood (72 commits!). It's kind of a miracle that everything still seems to work -- there's absolutely no way this revamp would have been possible without a solid testing system.

Here are some of the more visible changes that weren't previously mentioned:
* opts() is now deprecated, in favor of theme().
* opts(title='mytitle') is now deprecated. Instead use labs(title='mytitle'), or ggtitle('mytitle').
* theme_update() and update_element() are deprecated.

-Winston

Good question... I'm not totally sure, but I think the % signs just indicate that it's an infix operator. There are built-in operators (+, *, /, etc) that don't require the % signs around them.

>

NULL indicates that the property inherits from above. When the element properties are calculated with inheritance, all properties must be non-NULL; otherwise it throws an error.

> calc_element('axis.text.x', theme_grey(), verbose = TRUE)
axis.text.x --> axis.text
axis.text --> text
text --> nothing (top level)

 $ face      : chr "plain"

 $ colour    : chr "grey50"
 $ size      : num 9.6
 $ hjust     : num 0.5
 $ vjust     : num 1

 $ angle     : num 0
 $ lineheight: num 0.9
 - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

> mytheme <- theme_grey() %+replace% theme(text = element_text(colour='red'))
> mytheme$text
List of 8
 $ family    : NULL
 $ face      : NULL
 $ colour    : chr "red"
 $ size      : NULL
 $ hjust     : NULL
 $ vjust     : NULL
 $ angle     : NULL
 $ lineheight: NULL
 - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "element" "element_text"

> calc_element('axis.text.x', mytheme, verbose = TRUE)
axis.text.x --> axis.text
axis.text --> text
text --> Error in FUN("text"[[1L]], ...) :

  Theme element 'text' has NULL property: family, face, size, hjust, vjust, angle, lineheight

 With the + operator, there's actually no way to set an element property to NULL. (This can be done with the %+replace% operator, though.)

While it may sound a bit limiting to not be able to un-set properties with +, in practice I think it's a good tradeoff for simplicity. Here's an example: in theme_grey, the colour of 'text' is black, but the colour of 'axis.text' is grey50. With the + operator, you can't set axis.text$colour to NULL. You can set it to black, however, and I think that's good enough for most people.

If people want to do fancy stuff like un-setting properties, they can use the %+replace% operator. This would probably be used only by people who are creating their own themes.

-Winston

>

Sorry, this doesn't set mytheme$axis.text.y$angle to NULL.

Implementing this sort of behavior would make other things a lot more complicated. That is -- the behavior when adding an element_text to another element_text should not be defined in the element itself, but by the operator.

For example, suppose you decide to implement something like this:
theme_grey() + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle = NULL))    # No effect
theme_grey() + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(angle = reset_to_NULL))  # Reset angle when added

Then the elements (which are just lists) must be able to carry two different values for $angle: one which means "inherit", and one which means, "when this element is added to another element, reset this property so that it inherits". This is something that is better handled outside the element.

I've updated the wiki page:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/New-theme-system

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: why not qplot(mpg ~wt, data=mtcars)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am ccing the dev list serv too on this.  I do not think there is any
reason it could not be done in ggplot2, but I wonder how much it would
add.  It is nice for your example: plot(y ~  x), but beyond that, it
struggles a bit, I think.  If it were to be added, I thinking drawing
on lattice would be sensible, but even adding | only gets you a
couplel variables and facetting. To map additional variables to
colour, shape, line type, size, etc., I wonder if the formula
interface is complex enough?

In any case, I think it is worth having a discussion about.  It would
not even need to be implemented in ggplot2 necessarily.  Another
package (such as ggExtra) could upgrade qplot to generic, and define
methods.  A (very simple) example showing that it is not difficult to
hack something together to do this:

qplot.formula <- function(formula, ...) {
  args <- list(...)
  stopifnot(identical(length(formula), 3L))
  f <- formula[-1]
  p <- do.call("qplot", c(list(x = f[[2]], y = f[[1]]), args))
  return(invisible(p))
}

require(ggplot2)
## example 1
p <- qplot.formula(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)
print(p)

## can be extend as usual
print(p + stat_smooth())

## example 2
p2 <- qplot.formula(y ~ x, data = diamonds)
print(p2)

## works with variables in the global environment too
y <- mtcars$mpg
x <- mtcars$hp
p3 <- qplot.formula(y ~ x)
print(p3)

## lattice for demonstration
require(lattice)
xyplot(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)
xyplot(mpg ~ hp | cyl, data = mtcars)

How much demand is there for a formula interface?  Would people just
want it in qplot?  Part of me thinks that would just add confusion
between working with qplot and ggplot if one accepts formulae and the
other does not.  On the other hand, a simple formula interface may
ease new comers to ggplot2, as qplot already does, but it would follow
fairly sensibly then from any introduction of most basic modelling
functions.

f <- mpg ~ factor(cyl)

p4 <- qplot.formula(f, data = mtcars, geom = c("boxplot", "jitter"))
print(p4)

summary(lm(f, data = mtcars))

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: New 2d stat/geom thoughts
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I was playing around with some tessellation stuff yesterday and thought that, in addition to looking cool, some of the same visuals could be useful in a variety of situations.  Maybe someone who has some time would want implement them as stats/geoms.

Without further explanation, see code below, which culminates in the attached plot.  The stats/geoms I refer to are pretty obvious.

Cheers
david.

library(ggplot2)
library(deldir)
library(scales)
library(reshape2)
library(plyr)

# make fake points
n <- 50
k <- 4
mat <- cbind(rnorm(n), rnorm(n))
df <- as.data.frame(mat)
names(df) <- c('x','y')
qplot(x, y, data = df)

# convex hull
hull <- chull(df)
hullPointsIndices <- c(hull, hull[1])
hullPoly_df <- df[hullPointsIndices,]

qplot(x, y, data = df) +
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = 'red',
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 1)

# triangulate
xrng <- expand_range(range(df$x), .05)
yrng <- expand_range(range(df$y), .05)
deldir <- deldir(df, rw = c(xrng, yrng))

qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_segment( # polygons would be nicer...
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .5,
    data = deldir$delsgs, colour = 'red', alpha = .5
  )

# triangulate with polygons
trilist <- unclass(triang.list(deldir))
tridf <- melt(trilist, id.vars = c('x','y'))[,c(3,1:2)]
names(tridf) <- c('tri','x','y')

qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x=x, y=y, fill=factor(tri)),
    data = tridf, colour = 'black', alpha = .5
  ) +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE)

# voronoi
qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))

# voronoi with polygons
tilelist <- unclass(tile.list(deldir))
tilelist <- lapply(tilelist, function(l){
  data.frame(x = l$x, y = l$y)
})
tiledf <- melt(tilelist, id.vars = c('x','y'))[,c(3,1:2)]
names(tiledf) <- c('tile','x','y')

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x = x, y = y, fill = factor(tile)),
    data = tiledf, colour = 'black', alpha = .5
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))

# all together now!
ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = 'red',
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 1) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$delsgs
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 5.75, alpha = .75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = 1:n), size = 3, colour = 'green') +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))

ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x = x, y = y, fill = factor(tile)),
    data = tiledf, alpha = .5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$delsgs
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) +
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = NA,
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 5.75, alpha = .75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = 1:n), size = 3, colour = 'green') +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))

Hi David,

It's a very useful stat to have for sure. I remember a discussion with
Hadley and the author of deldir. There's a similar function
panel.levelplot.voronoi in latticeExtra (with the option to switch to
a faster package for the Delaunay calculation).

Unfortunately, last time I looked (last week) this deldir() function
was atrociously slow on reasonable data sets (~1e5 points, I'm looking
at electric field distributions in the output of a finite element
modelling software that uses such irregular tesselations).

There's also the recent interface to the C Triangle library on
r-forge: https://r-forge.r-project.org/R/?group_id=1077
I was in contact with the author when he started the project, and I
think he added some functionality to output the tesselation in a
format suitable for plotting.

Keep me updated if you're working on it!

Thanks,

baptiste

PS: The geom + stat is in the wiki wishlist:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/wishlist---feature-requests

Hi Brandon!

> Just out of curiosity, what sort of data is this for and what does the plot mean?

Well, the data in the email is fake (obviously).  But the Voronoi diagrams, for example, are useful in spatial stats as well as things like knn.  Baptiste's example of the finite element method is a cool one, and is actually general to any kind of mesh not just FEM applications.

Or the convex hull.  That's essentially the same as geom/stat_density2d, with the exception that it isn't calculating a contour of the density but it's convex support.  So you could have a stat_chull, or geom_chull, or maybe both as in density2d (at this point the division seems pretty blurry...), or perhaps it'd depend on the contour stuff; I'd just have to look at it.

Does that help?
